items.title: Three studies from Meta and AMI Labs back Yann LeCun's bet on JEPA world models over large language models
items.desc: Yann LeCun is pushing forward with his alternative to language models through his startup AMI Labs. The JEPA architecture aims to give machines an internal world model that captures cause and effect. Three new studies show progress in robot planning, more efficient training, and error correction, though the pieces still need to grow together. The article Three studies from Meta and AMI Labs back Yann LeCun's bet on JEPA world models over large language models appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Three studies from Meta and AMI Labs back Yann LeCun's bet on JEPA world models over large language models GPT-Image-2.6 prompted by THE DECODER AI pioneer Yann LeCun doesn't believe language models alone will lead to human-like intelligence. With his JEPA architecture, he is pursuing machines that model cause and effect and plan their actions in advance. Three new studies show how the pieces of this project fit together and where physics still sets limits. In late 2025, Yann LeCun left Meta after shaping its AI research for 12 years. He cited the company's growing focus on large language models as one reason, then co-founded the Paris startup AMI Labs and raised more than $1 billion. While much of the tech industry trains increasingly large chatbots, LeCun is focusing on systems for robotics, industry, and wearable devices intended to operate in the physical world. items.title: Hackers breached the US Air Force's flagship Cloud One platform, report says
items.desc: Hackers breached the US Air Force's flagship cloud platform. The article Hackers breached the US Air Force's flagship Cloud One platform, report says appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Hackers breached the US Air Force's flagship cloud platform. Reuters reports that attackers penetrated Cloud One, the Air Force's central cloud infrastructure, potentially exposing sensitive tactical, personnel, and logistics data. The breach was discovered last month during routine system upgrades. According to one source, the attackers exploited a software vulnerability to gain access to the platform's control plane. Cloud One has pooled cloud resources from Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle, and Alphabet since 2017, running applications that include air defense radar and munitions management. In response, the Air Force paused migration of additional applications, blocked updates, and revoked administrator privileges. US Cyber Command is assessing the damage. The breach comes amid growing concern about AI-powered attacks, as AI models can rapidly identify vulnerabilities across large cloud networks. At least six other cyber incidents have hit US government agencies recently, and Microsoft's cybersecurity division reported widespread use of the AI tool ARTEX . Who carried out the attack and whether any data was exfiltrated remain unknown. Ad Ad Already a subscriber? Sign in

items.title: Using light-dark() without getting caught out
items.desc: I honestly hadn't thought about "getting caught" by light-dark() — particularly when leaning heavily on it for this site — but Martin Underhill explains the user and rendering considerations, making me reflect on my choices as well. Using light-dark() without getting caught out originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.full: NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. I honestly hadn’t thought about “getting caught” by light-dark() — particularly when leaning heavily on it for this site — but Martin Underhill explains : Without fallbacks, browsers that don’t support light-dark() typically use black text on a white background in Light Mode, and white text on a dark grey background in Dark Mode. They’re not the exact colours I’d want, but my website looks fine. Again, it’s risky, so test thoroughly. Like Martin, I initially began implementing color themes based on media queries sniffing out user preferences. But it became super cumbersome to write prefers-color-scheme time and again. I mean, totally DX-world problems. I also remembered the piece Sara Joy wrote with us a while back encouraging a jump into the light-dark() waters and thought it’d be nice to take that advice. Doing that, I ran into another DX annoyance: writing two color values for each light-dark() . CSS variables help, of course, but even then it exhausted me. That says something more about me than the feature, but I digress. So, I took Martin’s process one step further to abstract all the things: :root { --gray-1: #eaeaea; /* Light */ /* ... */ --gray-10: #111; /* Dark */ --text: light-dark(var(--gray-1), var(--gray-10)); } .article-content { color: var(--text); } Very nice, at least for my penchant for laziness. But I ran into another issue because sometimes text needs to go the other direction. Keep abstracting. I could define the background variable which is normally the contrast to text: :root { --gray-1: #eaeaea; /* Light */ /* ... */ --gray-10: #111; /* Dark */ --text: light-dark(var(--gray-1), var(--gray-10)); --surface: light-dark(var(--gray-10), var(--gray-1)); } .widget-content { color: var(--surface); } Works, but using a helper called “surface” on a property controlling color bothers me too. I may be lazy, but I’m a little anal with semantics. Hence: :root { --gray-1: #eaeaea; /* Light */ /* ... */ --gray-10: #111; /* Dark */ --text: light-dark(var(--gray-1), var(--gray-10)); --text-reverse: light-dark(var(--gray-10), var(--gray-1)); } .article-content { color: var(--text-reverse); /* Light then dark */ } .widget-content { color: var(--text-reverse); /* Dark then light */ } …where “reverse” means it goes the opposite direction of a normal “light-dark” call and the “dark” value is called first. But even that is still too much for my brain to handle because now I’m left with multiple tokens to remember if I want things to be super semantic: :root { --gray-1: #eaeaea; /* Light */ /* ... */ --gray-10: #111; /* Dark */ --text: light-dark(var(--gray-1), var(--gray-10)); --text-reverse: light-dark(var(--gray-10), var(--gray-1)); --surface: light-dark(var(--gray-1), var(--gray-10)); --surface-reverse: light-dark(var(--gray-10), var(--gray-1)); } .article-content { background-color: var(--surface); /* Dark then light */ color: var(--text-reverse); /* Light then dark */ } .widget-content { background-color: var(--surface-reverse); /* Light then dark */ color: var(--text-reverse); /* Dark then light */ } so I went with an even more general abstraction: :root { --gray-1: #eaeaea;

items.title: Rockstar's AI dilemma: Can GTA 6's staggered release model survive coding agents?
items.desc: More than 40 projects are working to bring a leaked Xbox build of GTA 6 to PC through reverse engineering just days after its $3.79 billion record console launch. AI coding agents like Claude Code are speeding up the process so much that an early unofficial multiplayer mode is already running. Rockstar's delayed PC business model is coming under pressure. The article Rockstar's AI dilemma: Can GTA 6's staggered release model survive coding agents? appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Easy Perspectives Terms Own question Key Points Following a leak, developers are porting GTA 6 to PC through reverse engineering. They are using AI coding tools to speed up the work. Tracking data shows rapid progress across dozens of projects. Some already boot the game and show early multiplayer features. The unofficial builds threaten Rockstar's business model, while legal action against decentralized groups has little effect. Days after GTA 6's record console launch, numerous projects are working to bring a leaked Xbox build to PC. AI coding agents are dramatically speeding up reverse engineering and shaking up Rockstar's business model. A core pillar of Rockstar's business strategy is under pressure just days after Grand Theft Auto VI went on sale. The game had a historic debut on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S with an estimated $3.79 billion in first-day revenue. But a day later, the hacking group CyberLeek distributed a stolen Xbox image of the game, and the executable itself leaked a few days ago. Since then, a fast-moving scene of developers and modders has sprung up to get the game running on Windows through reverse engineering, compatibility layers, and recompilation. AI coding tools like Anthropic's Claude Code are driving that pace. Instead of spending months manually analyzing code and rebuilding console functions, developers are handing off much of the porting work to AI agents. One group even livestreamed the process. A tracking platform lists 40 active projects less than four days after the executable leaked. Nearly half of them can boot the game on PC. On the platform's own rating scale, the furthest project is more than 90 percent of the way to a playable PC build. Some projects are trying to add features including native ray-traced lighting. Gameplay footage of an unofficial PC multiplayer mode surfaced on November 26, and the platform's operator verified it. It shows multiple players moving through the game world with vehicles and voice chat at 25 to 30 frames per second. GTA 6 has officially launched only as a single-player title, and an online mode has no release date yet. There is no finished PC version ready for the general public yet. The most stable builds are incomplete, circulate in closed groups, or require substantial technical know-how. Even so, this pace breaks a decades-old assumption in the gaming industry. Console emulators often took years after a hardware generation launched, and brand-new blockbusters rarely ran on them soon after release. Rockstar and parent company Take-Two face more than a technical nuisance. The studio traditionally releases its flagship games on consoles first and follows with PC versions much later. GTA V took about 19 months to reach PC, and Red Dead Redemption 2 took about a year. So far, there is no official PC release date for GTA 6. That approach cuts optimization work at launch and encourages impatient players to buy the game twice. The online business is an even bigger vulnerability. items.title: SAP plans to cut at least 10,000 jobs as it pivots to AI
items.desc: SAP is preparing to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as part of a sweeping AI restructuring, Bloomberg reports, citing people familiar with the matter. The article SAP plans to cut at least 10,000 jobs as it pivots to AI appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: SAP is preparing to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as part of a sweeping AI restructuring, Bloomberg reports, citing people familiar with the matter. That's at least nine percent of the company's global workforce of more than 110,000. Every department has been asked to identify savings, with product development, engineering, and sales taking the biggest hit. The final number hasn't been set and could change after negotiations with employee representatives. In Germany, where about a quarter of SAP's workforce is based, a job guarantee runs through 2028. CEO Christian Klein wants to embed AI tools across SAP's product lineup. The company already cut roughly 10,000 jobs in 2024. Its competitors are making similar moves. Oracle slashed 21,000 positions over twelve months , and Microsoft is offering buyouts to around 60,000 employees . SAP declined to comment on the potential cuts, saying only that it reviews its organizational structure on an ongoing basis. The company recently announced a partnership with Mistral AI and has acquired several startups . Already a subscriber? Sign in

items.title: Former OpenAI researcher says the Riemann proof matters less than the fact that an AI system can produce it
items.desc: Complexity theorist and former OpenAI researcher Scott Aaronson argues that AI's recent math breakthroughs matter far beyond academia. The possible consequences, he writes, range from reshaping the global economy to threatening all life on Earth. He's also "virtually certain" that AI labs are sitting on "one or more bombshells" in cryptography. The article Former OpenAI researcher says the Riemann proof matters less than the fact that an AI system can produce it appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: In a blog post, complexity theorist and former OpenAI researcher Scott Aaronson lays out what AI's recent math breakthroughs might mean for the rest of us. Proving the Riemann hypothesis probably wouldn't change anyone's daily life, Aaronson writes. The ideas behind work like that could lead to new applications in science and engineering down the road, but it's anyone's guess which ones. Aaronson, a professor at the University of Texas at Austin, argues the far bigger deal is that AI can do this kind of work at all. In his view, that could have "staggering implications for everyday life," from reshaping the global economy to threatening all life on Earth. "Opinions differ," he writes, but anyone serious about the topic should set aside the "'ooga booga, me only care about Riemann proof if it help me make sharper spear' caveman act." Ad Aaronson walks through an OpenAI proof about matrix multiplication. The core question is how fast computational cost grows as matrices get larger. The new result, he writes, adds a matching lower bound to an existing fast algorithm. That shows how far computational cost can actually drop, at least in the model OpenAI studied. Ad OpenAI got a similar result for the Fourier transform, a basic math tool behind audio, image, and signal processing. It found a faster way to compute it and also proved that it can't be done much faster. Proofs like that second one are called lower bounds, and Aaronson stresses them in particular. A new method only sets a record, but a lower bound shows where further improvements hit a hard limit. It's now obvious that we'll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we'd previously only glimpsed through fog. Ad The results have also changed Aaronson's outlook on the biggest open question in his field. That question, known as P versus NP , asks whether every problem whose answer computers can check quickly can also be solved quickly. Most researchers suspect the answer is no, but nobody has proved it. "I now feel in my bones, for the first time ever, that a proof of P ≠ NP is not far," Aaronson writes. Such a proof would confirm that some problems are easy for computers to check but hard to solve. He adds that he's "virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources," that AI labs are sitting on "one or more bombshells" in cryptography, but says he doesn't have the details yet. Aaronson wrote in October that AI labs were testing whether their models could break cryptographic systems. Ad Already a subscriber? Sign in

items.title: Banned Nvidia Blackwell chips turn up in a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, Bloomberg reports
items.desc: Two Chinese companies installed Nvidia's powerful Blackwell chips at a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, according to a Bloomberg investigation. A serial number led Bloomberg to Taiwanese manufacturer Gigabyte. Exporting these chips to China without a US license is illegal. The article Banned Nvidia Blackwell chips turn up in a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, Bloomberg reports appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: It's no surprise at this point, but for the record: Two Chinese companies installed Nvidia's powerful Blackwell chips at a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, who had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The details come from documents filed with Chinese regulators and reviewed by Bloomberg . According to the filings, Shanghai Shuoyao offered a GB300-NVL72 rack as collateral for a 96 million yuan ($14 million) loan from Shanghai Innovation Bank, while a second company, Shanghai Kezhan, listed a GB200 server at the same site in loan documents. Exporting these chips to China without a US license is banned. Bloomberg traced the rack to Taiwanese manufacturer Gigabyte through a serial number in a public warranty database. Shanghai Shuoyao is closely tied to Singapore-based Megaspeed, according to Bloomberg. The Trump administration added Megaspeed to a US trade blacklist this month on suspicion of chip smuggling. Alice Huang founded Megaspeed in 2023 , and Nvidia approved it as a partner within four days. It went on to become Nvidia's largest customer in Southeast Asia, Bloomberg reported. items.title: OpenAI is building "Athena" data platform to cut down on AI agent guesswork
items.desc: OpenAI's data agent in ChatGPT Work still isn't accurate enough. Under the codename "Athena," the company is building a semantic layer that gives agents standardized definitions for business metrics. The tool could also put OpenAI in direct competition with Snowflake and Databricks. The article OpenAI is building "Athena" data platform to cut down on AI agent guesswork appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: OpenAI is building a data management platform codenamed "Athena" to make its AI agents more accurate when working with business data. Athena resembles a semantic layer, software that provides consistent definitions for business metrics such as revenue and customer count, The Information reports . The report says at least one customer found that ChatGPT Work's data analysis agent, launched last fall, wasn't accurate enough. The idea is to give agents the context they need so they guess less. A person familiar with the plans says OpenAI is using Athena to build agents that collect, document, and update business rules, so other agents don't have to start from scratch every time. Data platforms such as Snowflake and Databricks already offer their own semantic layers. Athena could be an effort to build a stronger competitive advantage, since the report says it's harder to switch semantic layer providers than to switch AI models. The platform is still in early development, and OpenAI hasn't shared a timeline or pricing. Ad Ad Already a subscriber? Sign in

items.title: Nvidia hits pause on chip shipments to Southeast Asia
items.desc: Nvidia has told manufacturing partners to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia as the U.S. tightens its push to keep AI chips out of China.
items.full: Nvidia is under pressure to do things differently, and a new WSJ report shows how far that’s going. According to the Journal, Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to hit pause on server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia for an unspecified period as it assesses whether its regional partners are meeting U.S. export requirements. As for why those countries, Chinese companies have been tapping Nvidia chips remotely from data centers there, a loophole the US Commerce Department closed — reportedly grudgingly — earlier this month. The Journal notes that the think tank Institute for Progress estimates remote data centers like these supply about 24% of China’s AI computing power.
